title: The Secret Geometry of Foldable Screens
subtitle: Why multi-link teardrop hinges solve the impossible physics of bending glass without snapping it—and how floating support plates eliminate the crease.
subject: Product Dives

neutral_axis.title: Neutral Axis & Strain Distribution
neutral_axis.body:
The neutral axis is the longitudinal surface within a bending structural sheet where longitudinal normal stress and strain are zero. When a composite laminate bends, outer layers undergo extreme tensile stress while inner layers experience compression.

Peak Bending Strain:
$$\epsilon_{\text{max}} = \frac{y}{\rho} = \frac{t}{2\rho}$$
$t$ is total stack thickness • $\rho$ is radius of curvature • $y$ is distance from neutral axis

In foldable displays, shifting the neutral axis toward the brittle Ultra-Thin Glass (UTG) layer prevents tensile fracture.

utg_fracture.title: UTG Critical Griffith Flaw Criterion
utg_fracture.body:
Ultra-Thin Glass (30–50 μm) is chemically strengthened via potassium-sodium ion exchange ($K^+ \leftrightarrow Na^+$) to generate a deep surface compressive stress layer ($> 700\text{ MPa}$). However, sub-micron edge micro-cracks dictate brittle failure under tension.

Griffith Fracture Criterion:
$$\sigma_f = \frac{K_{IC}}{\sqrt{\pi \cdot a_c}}$$
$K_{IC} \approx 0.72\text{ MPa}\sqrt{\text{m}}$ • Critical defect size $a_c < 0.35\,\mu\text{m}$ • Tensile failure occurs when $\sigma_{\text{applied}} > \sigma_f$

Reducing bending curvature $\rho$ keeps operating tensile stress safely below the Griffith threshold.

hertzian_stress.title: Hertzian Cam-Follower Contact Stress
hertzian_stress.body:
Hertzian contact stress governs the localized compressive stress field formed when two curved metallic surfaces are pressed together under heavy spring preload in the hinge torque engine.

Max Hertzian Contact Pressure:
$$P_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{F_N \cdot E^*}{\pi \cdot R_{\text{eff}} \cdot L}}$$
$F_N$ is normal cam preload • $R_{\text{eff}}$ is equivalent curvature radius • $E^*$ is effective contact modulus

If $P_{\text{max}}$ exceeds the shakedown limit of the carburized steel (typically $1{,}600\text{ MPa}$), micro-spalling occurs, causing hinge grittiness.

mim_feedstock.title: MIM Catalytic Debinding & Sintering
mim_feedstock.body:
Metal Injection Molding (MIM) blends 17-4 PH stainless steel powder (particle size 4–15 μm) with a polyacetal (POM) thermoplastic binder to produce feedstock injected into multi-cavity tooling.

Isotropic Sintering Shrinkage:
$$L_{\text{sintered}} = L_{\text{green}} \cdot (1 - \alpha)$$
Linear shrinkage $\alpha \approx 16.5\% \pm 0.15\%$ • Sintering temperature: $1{,}340^\circ\text{C}$ in pure dry hydrogen

High-temperature vacuum sintering dissolves pores, yielding $> 98.5\%$ theoretical density and $\pm 10\,\mu\text{m}$ dimensional tolerances on miniature gear teeth.

oca_viscoelasticity.title: Optically Clear Adhesive (OCA) Viscoelastic Relaxation
oca_viscoelasticity.body:
Optically Clear Adhesive (OCA) layers (25–50 μm) bond display layers while permitting inter-laminar slip during folding. Under prolonged closure, the adhesive exhibits time-dependent stress relaxation.

Prony Series Shear Relaxation:
$$G(t) = G_\infty + \sum_{i=1}^N G_i \exp\left(-\frac{t}{\tau_i}\right)$$
$G_\infty$ is equilibrium modulus • $\tau_i$ are relaxation time constants (0.1s to $10^5$s)

If OCA relaxes excessively while closed, it cannot exert sufficient elastic restoring force upon opening, causing a visible display crease.

article_html:
ISSUE #004•PRODUCT DIVES•14 MIN READ

The Secret Geometry of Foldable Screens

Why multi-link teardrop hinges solve the impossible physics of bending glass without snapping it—and how floating support plates eliminate the crease.

1. The Neutral Axis Dilemma & Beam Bending Mechanics

A foldable smartphone is an engineering paradox: it demands that brittle silicate glass, copper foil circuitry, and optically clear polymers withstand hundreds of thousands of sharp $180^\circ$ bends without shattering, delaminating, or forming a permanent plastic trench.

When a multi-layer composite sheet is folded, its cross-section is divided by the neutral axis—the plane where longitudinal normal stress and axial strain equal zero. Across any cross-section of total thickness $t$ bent to a radius of curvature $\rho$, the peak longitudinal strain $\epsilon_{\text{max}}$ at the extreme outer and inner fibers is governed by Euler-Bernoulli beam kinematics:

$$\epsilon_{\text{max}} = \frac{y}{\rho} = \frac{t}{2\rho}$$

Where $y = t/2$ represents the distance from the neutral axis to the outermost surface. In first-generation foldable devices, industrial designers utilized a traditional U-shaped hinge. To minimize the phone's closed thickness, the U-shaped fold forced the display stack into an aggressive bend radius of $\rho = 1.25\text{ mm}$ to $1.50\text{ mm}$.

For an ultra-thin display laminate measuring $t = 0.42\text{ mm}$ (encompassing the PET protective liner, polarizer film, 30 μm Ultra-Thin Glass (UTG), OLED emitter matrix, and stainless steel backplate), evaluating the induced strain reveals the failure mode:

$$\epsilon_{\text{U-shape}} = \frac{0.42\text{ mm}}{2 \cdot (1.25\text{ mm})} = 0.168 \quad (16.8\%\text{ tensile / compressive strain})$$

This magnitude of mechanical strain is catastrophic. While flexible polymers can elastically accommodate $3\%$ to $5\%$ strain, silicate glass possesses a theoretical elastic limit of only $7\%$ under pristine laboratory vacuum, and an effective production yield limit of under $2.2\%$ due to surface Griffith micro-flaws. Subjecting UTG to $16.8\%$ strain guarantees rapid crack nucleation, delamination of the Optically Clear Adhesive (OCA), and catastrophic fracture along the hinge centerline within 2,000 to 5,000 duty cycles.

The Teardrop (Waterdrop) Kinematic Breakthrough:
To solve this fundamental limitation without expanding the phone's closed thickness, hardware architects abandoned the concentric circle fold in favor of the Euler clothoid or teardrop geometry. Instead of squeezing the screen tightly along the seam, the teardrop hinge drops internal mechanical support plates inward, allowing the bent portion of the display to balloon into a bulbous internal cavity while the outer housing folds completely parallel ($0^\circ$ gap).

By expanding the internal bend radius to $\rho \ge 3.40\text{ mm}$, the peak bending strain collapses by more than half:

$$\epsilon_{\text{teardrop}} = \frac{0.42\text{ mm}}{2 \cdot (3.40\text{ mm})} = 0.0617 \quad (6.17\%\text{ strain})$$

Coupled with neutral-axis positioning layers (shifting the zero-strain line directly into the neutral plane of the brittle glass core), peak strain in the UTG drops below 1.1%—well within its infinite fatigue endurance regime ($> 400{,}000$ cycles).

FIG 02 — FOLD GEOMETRY COMPARISON: Side-by-side comparison of legacy U-shaped concentric bending versus the Euler clothoid teardrop fold, illustrating how the internal waterdrop loop relieves tensile strain on Ultra-Thin Glass while enabling flush closure. SCHEMATIC: KINEMATIC CAD
FIG 03 — THE 4-STAGE TEARDROP KINEMATIC SEQUENCE PLANAR (180°) → BENDING → SLIDING → CLOSED (0°)
STAGE 01: 180° FLAT
Planar Substrate Lockout

Floating support wings are locked flush with the chassis by secondary cam detents, forming a rigid 0.10 mm substrate beneath the UTG that resists stylus and finger indentation.

STAGE 02: 120° UNLATCH
Floating Plate Descent

As rotation begins, dual synchronization gears drive guide pins along an angled track, dropping the center support plates vertically by 1.35 mm into the housing spine.

STAGE 03: 60° BENDING
Teardrop Cavity Expansion

With support plates recessed, the screen enters free-loop deflection. The lateral sliders begin stroking outward along precision curved tracks to absorb display arc-length differential.

STAGE 04: 0° CLOSED
Zero-Gap Waterdrop Lock

The housing halves meet parallel with zero gap. The screen loops into a bulbous 3.4 mm waterdrop with <1.1% glass strain, while sliders hold ΔL = 1.42 mm tension balance.

FIG 03 — KINEMATIC SEQUENCE: The four-phase transition of a teardrop hinge mechanism, demonstrating the synchronized vertical descent of central support wings and the lateral translation of perimeter sliders. FLOWCHART 01

2. Path-Length Mechanics: Absorbing the Arc-Length Differential (ΔL)

While the teardrop loop eliminates excessive tensile strain, it creates an aggressive kinematic constraint: Path-Length Mismatch ($\Delta L$).

When a smartphone unfolds from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$, the screen is a flat plane spanning width $W_0$. However, when folded into a teardrop shape inside a closed chassis, the curved profile traces an elastica curve composed of a central circular arc of radius $\rho$ flanked by two inflection fillets of radius $r_i$. The total contour length $S$ of the curved display path is given by:

$$S = \int_0^{\theta_{\text{max}}} \rho(\theta) \, d\theta + 2 \int_0^{\phi} r_i(\phi) \, d\phi$$

Because the chassis frame is rigid and fixed to the hinge rotation pins, the distance along the outer perimeter differs from the inner neutral axis by a geometric stroke:

$$\Delta L = S_{\text{curved}} - L_{\text{flat}} \approx 1.25\text{ mm} - 1.65\text{ mm}$$

If the display were anchored firmly to both sides of the chassis without compliance, this $\Delta L$ differential would induce violent mechanical stress:

  • During Folding (Tensile Delamination): The screen stack would be pulled taut over the hinge spine like a guitar string, creating normal peel stresses exceeding the $0.8\text{ MPa}$ adhesive shear bond of the OCA and ripping the display away from its digitizer.
  • During Unfolding (Compressive Buckling): Excess material would be shoved into the seam under compressive thrust, causing the UTG to buckle upward, generating the permanent high-amplitude "crease trench" that plagues inferior foldables.

The Multi-Link Synchronized Slider Solution:
Modern teardrop hinges solve this by mounting the display support plates onto lateral sliding carriages. These carriages ride on precision curved tracks machined directly into the outer wing frames. As the hinge closes, a multi-link scissor mechanism pulls the left and right display wings outward by exactly $\Delta L / 2 \approx 0.71\text{ mm}$ each, absorbing the length change with zero net tension.

FIG 04 — MULTI-LINK TEARDROP HINGE KINEMATIC CROSS-SECTION DUAL SLIDER STROKE: ΔL = 1.42 mm • CAM PRELOAD: 45 N • ZERO-GAP PROFILE
FIG 04 — CAD SCHEMATIC: Transverse kinematic section view of the multi-link teardrop hinge mechanism, highlighting the synchronized spur gears, lateral slider translation, and the vertical drop path of the internal support wings. SCHEMATIC: CAD ARCHIVE

3. The Torque Engine: Helical Cams & "Flex Mode" Detents

A folding phone must not merely open and close; it must deliver a luxurious, tuned tactile resistance across its entire sweep. Users demand a decisive "snap" into the $180^\circ$ flat state, an effortless glide during closure, and the ability to hold any arbitrary angle between $45^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ (often marketed as "Flex Mode" or "Hover Stance") for hands-free video recording.

This tactile curve is generated by the Torque Engine—an assembly of multi-lobed helical cams preloaded by miniature Belleville disc spring washers or high-tensile music-wire coil springs.

Cam Kinematics & Torque Derivation:
As the user rotates the hinge through angle $\theta$, the follower rides along the inclined helical surface of the drive cam. The profile of the cam determines the axial displacement $z(\theta)$ of the springs. The instantaneous torque $T(\theta)$ opposing or assisting user motion is derived from the balance of spring force and friction:

$T_{\text{hold}} \approx \mu \cdot R_{\text{cam}} \cdot F_{\text{spring}}$

Where:

  • $R_{\text{cam}}$ is the mean pitch radius of the cam face ($2.10\text{ mm}$ to $2.85\text{ mm}$).
  • $F_{\text{spring}}(z) = k \cdot (z_0 + z(\theta))$ is the normal spring force, where initial preload $F_0 = k \cdot z_0 \approx 38\text{ N}$ to $48\text{ N}$.
  • $\alpha = \arctan\left(\frac{1}{R_{\text{cam}}} \cdot \frac{dz}{d\theta}\right)$ is the instantaneous cam helix angle.
  • $\mu$ is the dynamic coefficient of friction across the lubricated metal interface (typically $\mu \approx 0.08 - 0.12$).

Achieving the "Free-Stop" Hover Regime:
To achieve stable hovering without motorized locking pins, the mechanism relies on the Coulomb friction locking condition. In the intermediate angle window ($45^\circ \le \theta \le 120^\circ$), the cam slope is designed to be flat ($\frac{dz}{d\theta} = 0$, so $\alpha = 0$). The holding friction torque becomes:

$$T_{\text{hold}} = \mu \cdot R_{\text{cam}} \cdot F_{\text{spring}}$$

If the gravitational moment induced by the upper display half ($M_g = m \cdot g \cdot d_{\text{cg}} \cdot \sin\theta \approx 0.045\text{ Nm}$) is less than $T_{\text{hold}}$ ($0.065\text{ Nm}$), the phone remains locked at any arbitrary angle without sagging. As the phone approaches $180^\circ$, the follower enters a steep negative detent groove ($alpha < 0$), releasing stored spring energy to snap the chassis into a dead-flat plane with satisfying tactile feedback.

4. Manufacturing, Tooling & MIM Clearances

A modern teardrop hinge is composed of 45 to 85 precision components packaged into a spine cavity less than $3.8\text{ mm}$ deep. Tolerances that would be considered exceptional in watchmaking are strictly required here to prevent tactile "slop" or mechanical binding.

Tolerance Stack-Up & The 10-Micron Gate:
Because motion transmits through a kinetic chain of gears, pins, link plates, and cam followers, individual clearance errors accumulate rapidly. A tolerance stack-up analysis across 8 mating interfaces demonstrates that a dimensional variance of just $\pm 0.025\text{ mm}$ ($25\,\mu\text{m}$) per part generates over 0.35 mm of tip play at the phone's outer display bezel—causing the phone to feel loose, rattling, or misaligned.

To maintain a premium rigidity standard, primary hinge pins are centerless ground to $\pm 0.004\text{ mm}$ ($4\,\mu\text{m}$), while interlocking link carriages are produced via Metal Injection Molding (MIM) followed by secondary CNC diamond profiling of contact lands.

Tooling Steel Selection for MIM:
Injecting abrasive, metal-powder-loaded feedstock at $180^\circ\text{C}$ and $110\text{ MPa}$ causes severe abrasive tool wear. Mold cavities are machined from powdered-metallurgy hot-work tool steel (Böhler M390 Microclean or Uddeholm Elmax) vacuum hardened to 58–60 HRC and coated with Titanium Aluminum Nitride (TiAlN) physical vapor deposition (PVD) to resist wash-out across 500,000 shots.

5. Metallurgy, Hertzian Cam Stress & Tribology

The material selection for hinge components is governed by two conflicting requirements: extreme yield strength under compact packaging and tribological immunity to adhesive wear.

SUS630 / 17-4 PH Precipitation-Hardening Stainless Steel:
The structural core of the hinge—including the spine chassis, synchronization gears, and slider links—is molded from 17-4 PH stainless steel. After solvent debinding and hydrogen sintering, components undergo an H900 age-hardening heat treatment ($482^\circ\text{C}$ for 1 hour followed by air cooling).

This precipitates sub-microscopic copper-rich clusters throughout the martensitic matrix, driving ultimate tensile strength past 1,310 MPa with a Rockwell hardness of 43–45 HRC. This extreme strength prevents synchronization gear teeth from bending or shearing when the user forcefully closes the phone on an obstacle.

Managing Hertzian Cam Contact Stress:
The contact patch between the cam follower pin and the torque cam experiences severe Hertzian contact pressure:

$$P_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{F_N \cdot E^*}{\pi \cdot R_{\text{eff}} \cdot L}}$$

With a $45\text{ N}$ spring force concentrated onto an effective curvature radius of $R_{\text{eff}} = 1.1\text{ mm}$ across a contact line length of $L = 1.8\text{ mm}$, peak pressure surges to $P_{\text{max}} \approx 1{,}180\text{ MPa}$. Under cyclic sliding friction, raw stainless steel would suffer immediate adhesive micro-welding, surface galling, and metal transfer.

The Dry-Film Tribology Architecture:
Traditional liquid greases cannot be used inside phone hinges. Over time, liquid oils migrate outward via capillary action, dissolving display adhesives and collecting abrasive environmental pocket lint. Instead, manufacturers utilize bonded solid dry-film lubricants:

  • Diamond-Like Carbon (DLC): Cams are coated with a 2.5 μm thick layer of hydrogenated amorphous carbon (a-C:H), yielding a surface hardness $> 2{,}400\text{ HV}$ and a coefficient of friction $\mu \le 0.08$.
  • PTFE / MoS2 Impregnation: Sliding links are treated with microscopic fluoropolymer micro-coatings that self-burnish during the first 1,000 cycles, maintaining smooth, grit-free glide without attracting debris.
  • Micro-Fiber Bristle Sweepers: Tiny nylon sweepers ($0.04\text{ mm}$ bristle diameter) are sealed at the hinge-to-bezel gaps, mechanically clearing dust and sand grains every time the phone folds.

6. Empirical Torture Metrology & Crease Interferometry

Validating a next-generation teardrop hinge requires rigorous bench torture testing that compresses ten years of human abuse into four weeks of continuous automated cycling.

High-Speed Automated Cycling: Robotic pneumatically actuated test rigs cycle the hinge at $0.5\text{ Hz}$ (one complete open-and-close every two seconds) for 400,000 cycles—the equivalent of 100 folds per day for over 10 years. Continuous load-cell telemetry monitors torque degradation: if friction torque drifts by more than $\pm 15\%$, the test flags lubrication breakdown or galling.

Environmental Chambers (-20°C to +65°C): Because the aluminum chassis ($\alpha_{\text{Al}} \approx 23 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$) and steel hinge ($\alpha_{\text{steel}} \approx 11 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$) have vastly different thermal expansion coefficients, temperature extremes shrink operating clearances. Because aluminum contracts twice as fast as steel when cold, dropping down to -20°C shrinks the hinge clearances by up to 14 μm. If the initial manufacturing tolerance is not precisely compensated, the sliders will bind solid in freezing climates.

White-Light Optical Profilometry (Crease Metrology):
To quantify display crease severity, engineers scan the unfolded screen with a non-contact white-light interferometric optical profiler. The profilometer maps the micro-topography across a $40 \times 40\text{ mm}$ grid, measuring two decisive metrics:

  • Peak-to-Valley Trench Depth ($D_v$): Benchmark teardrop designs achieve $D_v < 32\,\mu\text{m}$ (versus $> 120\,\mu\text{m}$ on first-gen U-shape folds).
  • Maximum Slope Angle ($\theta_{\text{crease}}$): The human fingertip cannot detect height steps below $40\,\mu\text{m}$ if the transition slope is gradual. By spreading the deformation over a wide $12\text{ mm}$ span, the slope remains below $1.2^\circ$—rendering the crease visually invisible and tactilely undetectable during swipe gestures.
